title: Week 2a — LLM Foundations
text: Today we are going to run an LLM locally: a real open-weight model, on your laptop, no API key, no cloud.

title: Week 2a — LLM Foundations
text:
1. Install Ollama
Ollama is the tool we’ll use to download and run open-weight models.

macOSWindowsLinux


Download the app from ollama.com/download, drag it into Applications, and open it once. Then verify in Terminal:
ollama --version
If you use Homebrew, brew install ollama works too.


Download and run the installer from ollama.com/download. Then open PowerShell and verify:
ollama --version


One command:
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
Then verify:
ollama --version

title: Week 2a — LLM Foundations
text:
2. Download and run a model
We’ll use Qwen 3.5, an open-weight model family that comes in sizes from 0.8B to 122B parameters. One command downloads the default size (about 6.6 GB) and drops you into a chat:
ollama run qwen3.5
Type a message and watch it answer, token by token — that streaming is the autoregressive loop from lecture, live. Type /bye to exit the chat.
Pick a size that fits your machine. The default is a good middle ground, but if your laptop has 8 GB of RAM or you want a faster download, grab a smaller one; if you have a big machine, try a bigger one:
ollama run qwen3.5:2b     # small and quick — any laptop
ollama run qwen3.5:4b     # 8 GB RAM
ollama run qwen3.5:9b     # 16 GB RAM (the default)
ollama run qwen3.5:27b    # 32 GB+ RAM
The full list of sizes is on the model page. Rule of thumb: the download size is roughly the RAM the model needs while running.
Also grab these two for class. They are tiny (a few hundred megabytes each, seconds to download, run on anything) and we will use them together in a demonstration:
ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b        # instruction-tuned
ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b-base   # raw pretrained — no post-training
Same architecture, same size, same training data — the only difference is what happened after pretraining. Ask them both a question in class and you will see exactly what that difference buys. (ollama pull downloads without starting a chat; ollama run does both.)

title: Week 2a — LLM Foundations
text:
3. Commands you’ll actually use
ollama list        # models you have downloaded
ollama ps          # models currently loaded in memory
ollama rm qwen3.5  # delete a model and free the disk space
And inside a chat, /bye exits.

title: Week 2a — LLM Foundations
text:
Why we’re doing this
Ollama also runs a local API server (at localhost:11434), which means later in the course your agents can call a model that is entirely yours. We will use that for local inference.

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text: This page is a starting point for finding your final project idea. The areas and papers below are initial directions; the strongest projects usually come from a question you find yourself while reading. What follows first is the one rule that is not optional.

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text:
The rule
An application domain alone is not a research contribution. “We will build a travel-planning agent” is not a project. “We investigate whether explicit constraint tracking improves long-horizon planning agents under changing constraints” is. The domain is the testbed; the mechanism is the contribution. Every strong project fits this template:

agentic mechanism → experimental manipulation → measured agent behavior

For example: memory policy → preference updates → stale-action rate. Or: tool descriptions → distractor similarity → tool-selection accuracy.

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text:
What fits in a semester
Feasible: controlled experiments on existing or synthetic benchmarks · fine-tuning small open-weight models (LoRA on a 4–9B model is a weekend on some GPU) · trajectory analyses over logged runs · architectural comparisons under a fixed token budget.
Not feasible: pretraining a model · large-scale RL training · months of human data collection

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text:
Where to look

NeurIPS proceedings — including the Datasets & Benchmarks track, where most agent benchmarks are published
ICLR on OpenReview — reviews are public; reading them teaches you how the field argues
ICML proceedings
ACL Anthology — ACL, EMNLP, NAACL; most tool-use and agent-NLP work lands here
COLM — the LLM-focused venue; young, high signal
Workshops are the goldmine for project-scale ideas. Each year NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML host workshops on language agents, open-world agents, safe and trustworthy agents, and multi-agent systems. Workshop papers are shorter, newer, and closer to what a semester project can extend. Check the current workshop lists at neurips.cc, iclr.cc, and icml.cc, and search OpenReview for “agents” workshops.
For staying current: arXiv cs.CL and cs.AI, navigated with Semantic Scholar.

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text:
Starting directions
In what follows, we provide a few anchor papers per area. Read the anchors, then follow their citations forward on Semantic Scholar or Google Scholar to explore who cited this, and what they found wrong with it.

1. Benchmarking and evaluation
Task success alone poorly characterizes agents. Open questions: which trajectory features predict failure before a task ends, how many runs characterize reliability, how cost should enter benchmarks, and how reliable LLM-as-judge scoring really is.

τ²-bench — conversational tool-agents with a simulated user
SWE-bench — the coding-agent benchmark and its saturation story
Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? — a failure taxonomy worth extending
A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents
Holistic Agent Leaderboard — cost-aware evaluation



2. Fine-tuning small models for agentic tasks
Can a 4–9B open-weight model be made meaningfully better at tool calling, reflection, or planning with a modest fine-tune? This is squarely semester-sized: generate or collect traces, LoRA-tune, compare against prompting the same base model. (Pretraining is out of scope — see above.)

FireAct — fine-tuning on agent trajectories
AgentTuning — instruction-tuning for agent abilities
ToolLLM — training for large-scale API use
xLAM — a family of function-calling models
DeepSeek-R1 — see the distillation section: small models learning from reasoning traces



3. Agentic AI safety and security
Agent safety is not chatbot safety: the question is not “did the model say something harmful” but “what did the system actually do.” A strong architectural question from the idea doc: at which layer should prompt-injection defenses operate — model prompting, tool authorization, or execution monitoring?

Not What You’ve Signed Up For — indirect prompt injection, the founding paper
AgentDojo — an injection benchmark you can run
AgentHarm — measuring harmful task completion
Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL)
Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents



4. Tool use and MCP
Tool use looks solved in demos and is not solved scientifically. Selection is fragile to description wording, tool-set size, and near-duplicate distractors — and MCP adds questions about poisoning, permissions, and provenance.

Tool Preferences in Agentic LLMs are Unreliable — small description changes shift tool usage by more than 10×; a perfect paper to extend
What Are Tools Anyway? — the survey that maps the area
Gorilla — LLMs and massive API sets
Model Context Protocol: Landscape and Security

A clean experiment: give an agent 5, 20, 50, and 100 tools with progressively similar distractors, and measure selection accuracy, cost, and failure modes.


5. Memory and context
Older memory benchmarks test whether an agent can retrieve a fact; the open question is whether it uses remembered information appropriately when acting — and what it should forget.

Mem2ActBench - benchmark for evaluating long-term memory; can be easily extended
MemGPT — memory hierarchies
Generative Agents — memory in believable simulation
Mem0 and A-Mem — production memory systems

A clean experiment from the idea doc: compare append-everything, overwrite, recency-weighted, and conflict-aware memory policies as user preferences change; measure task success, stale-memory errors, and token cost.

title: Week 1 — Setup
text: Welcome to Agentic AI. There is no ICA this week. Your job before next week is small: install one editor, and work through the Python primer if your Python is rusty or new. Everything else, including Python itself, will be installed next week in one step.

title: Week 1 — Setup
text:
1. Install VS Code
VS Code is the editor we will use all semester for notebooks and code.

Download it from code.visualstudio.com and install it. On a Mac, drag the app into your Applications folder. On Windows, run the installer with the default options.
Open VS Code, click the Extensions icon in the left bar (four squares), and install two extensions, both published by Microsoft: Python and Jupyter.

That is the whole task. You do not need to configure anything else yet.

title: Week 1 — Setup
text:
2. Python primer
If you have not written much Python, or you have never seen things like TypedDict, list comprehensions, or decorators, work through the primer before Week 2. It assumes no prior Python and everything in it comes back later in the course.
The easiest way to run it is Google Colab, which runs the notebook in your browser with nothing to install. You will need a Google account.
Open the Python Primer in Colab
In Colab, run cells with Shift+Enter, top to bottom. Change things and rerun them. The primer ends with eight exercises. If those feel fine, you are ready for Week 2.
If you want to go deeper than the primer, the official Python tutorial is the best next stop. It is free, well written, and goes well beyond what we need. Chapters 3 through 5 line up with the primer if you want a second pass at the same ideas.

title: Week 1 — Setup
section: Do I need to install Python?
text:
Do I need to install Python?
Not yet. Next week we will set up the full course environment with a tool called uv, and it installs the right version of Python for you as part of one command. If you install Python on your own this week, you will not break anything, but you also will not need it, and having several Pythons on one machine is a common source of confusion. Wait for the Week 2 setup guide.

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
text:
Please follow these instructions carefully.
By the end you will have one folder that looks like this:

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
text:
1. Install uv
uv is a fast Python environment manager. It also installs Python itself, so you do not need to install Python separately — whatever Python you do or do not have on your machine, the result is the same.

macOSWindowsLinux


In Terminal:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
Then close and reopen the terminal, and verify:
uv --version


In PowerShell:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
Then close and reopen PowerShell, and verify:
uv --version


curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
Then close and reopen the terminal, and verify:
uv --version

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
text:
2. Create your course project
Make one folder for the whole course and open it in VS Code:
mkdir agentic-ai-course
cd agentic-ai-course
code .
If code is not recognized, open VS Code manually, then File, Open Folder.
From here on, run commands in VS Code’s integrated terminal (Terminal > New Terminal)  so you are always in the right place.

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
text:
3. Create the environment
From inside agentic-ai-course:
uv venv --python 3.13
This creates .venv, a self-contained Python 3.13 environment that lives in your project folder. Everything we install goes in here and nowhere else.

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
section: 4. Get the lecture files and install the dependencies
text:
4. Get the lecture files and install the dependencies
git clone https://github.com/agenticllms/agenticllms.github.io.git course-files
uv pip install -r course-files/lecture-files/requirements.txt
cp -r course-files/lecture-files/W02b W02b
The first command brings in the course repository — the class files live in its lecture-files/ folder (the rest is the course website; you can ignore it). The second installs every library the course uses into your .venv. Note there is no pip on its own anywhere in this course: it is always uv pip, which cannot install into the wrong Python. The third makes your working copy of today’s files.
Each class day, the process will involve the following: pull, then copy the day’s folder out and work in the copy.
cd course-files
git pull
cd ..
cp -r course-files/lecture-files/W03a W03a
(Windows PowerShell: Copy-Item -Recurse course-files/lecture-files/W03a W03a.)
Pulling is additive: it brings the new day’s folder and leaves previous days untouched. But here is the rule that keeps it that way: treat course-files as read-only and do your work in the copies. Running a notebook saves outputs into the file, which counts as a local edit, and local edits are what make a future git pull refuse. If course-files ever does get messy, reset it with git restore . from inside that folder — safe, because nothing of yours lives there.

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
text:
5. Add your API keys
Copy the template to your project root and rename it:
cp course-files/lecture-files/example.env .env
Open .env in VS Code and paste in your keys — GOOGLE_API_KEY and TAVILY_API_KEY will be required later; the others are optional. Never commit or share this file, and never paste a key into a notebook cell.

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
section: 6. Point VS Code at your environment
text:
6. Point VS Code at your environment
This is a crucial step:

Open any notebook from your W02b/ copy.
Click the kernel picker in the top-right corner of the notebook.
Choose the interpreter at agentic-ai-course/.venv (it may be listed as .venv (Python 3.13)).

VS Code remembers this per notebook. If a notebook ever complains that a module is missing, check the kernel picker before anything else — nine times out of ten the notebook is quietly running some other Python.

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
text:
7. Verify
Open W02b/W02b.1_LLM_API_Basics.ipynb and run the first cell. If it prints that the API key is loaded, you are done. If not, see below.

title: Week 2b — Course Environment Setup
text:
Some Common Errors








Symptom
Cause
Fix




ModuleNotFoundError
Notebook is on the wrong kernel
Kernel picker → choose .venv → restart kernel


pip: command not found
Bare pip is not on your PATH
Use uv pip install ... instead


No API key found
.env missing, misplaced, or kernel started before you created it
.env goes in the project root, next to .venv; then restart the kernel


Works in one notebook, not another
The two notebooks are on different kernels
Set both to .venv


uv: command not found right after install
Terminal opened before the install finished
Close and reopen the terminal


git pull refuses: local changes would be overwritten
You ran or edited notebooks inside course-files
cd course-files, then git restore ., then pull again. Work in copies from now on



Last, please keep in mind that environment problems are not a test of your ability; everyone hits them, including me.
